objectives: Separate what the Pharaoh believed about himself (“saw himself as a god”) from what the narrator tells us about his rule.
Trace the chain belief → fear → harsh decision → forced work with quoted evidence.

Notice how the chapter places the story in history and moves it on (in the 13th century BC, over 3000 years ago, At that time, Years passed, One day), and discover “feared that … would”, make + person + base verb, So / That’s why and continued to + verb.
Judge power by how it treats people, and name one fair alternative to a fear-based decision.
content.pedagogy: Start with time, not with the villain. Learners place the chapter’s time expressions on a board timeline, then build a two-row chain: What people believed (the Children of Israel / the Pharaoh) and what the Pharaoh did because of his fear. Grammar grows out of this chain: You ask “Did the group take control? What was the Pharaoh thinking about, the past or the future?” and learners discover that “would” is his future seen from the past before you name it.
priorKnowledge: Past simple of common verbs, “because” and “so”, and years and centuries in English (the 13th century BC).
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners may take “saw himself as a god” as narrator fact or treat the Pharaoh’s fear as a justification. The chapter presents his fear as the reason for oppression, not an excuse for it.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: placing the story in time (in the 13th century BC, over 3000 years ago, At that time) vs moving it on (Years passed, One day) · feared that … would (a future seen from the past) · make + person + base verb and the passive were made to · So / That’s why for a result (That’s because gives a reason) · continued to + base verb.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort the five time expressions. Ask only two questions: “Which ones tell us WHEN in history? Which ones make time jump forward?” Pairs explain “ago” (counting back from today) before you confirm it.
Build (Activities 2–3): before Activity 2 board “The Pharaoh feared that this group … would take control of his kingdom.” and ask “Did it happen? Is he thinking about the past or the future?” Then learners rewrite his thought with will and the forced work with “were made to”, and choose So / That’s why / to rule.
Likely errors: *before 3000 years (Turkish “3000 yıl önce”) · *feared that … will · *made them to do (active) · That’s because for a result · *continued rule.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a different historical situation with at least four patterns (At that time …, feared that … would …, That’s why …, made … + verb, continued to …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the fear sentence into three meaning units: “The PHARaoh FEARED | that this GROUP, which was LARger than the eGYPtians, | would take conTROL of his KINGdom.”
Time frames as single units with a pause after them: “At THAT time, |”, “YEARS PASSED | and …”, “One DAY | …”.
Numbers: “in the thirTEENTH CENtury B C”, “over THREE THOUsand years aGO”.
Word focus: PHA-raoh (/ˈfeə.rəʊ/), dic-ta-TO-ri-al, des-POT-ic, AN-ces-tor, IS-ra-el-ites. Weak “to” in “continued to RULE” (/tə/).
beforeReading: Draw a long line on the board from “today” back into the past. Ask: “How far back do you think this story happened?” Learners write a guess on a sticky note or in their notebook, then check it against the first lines.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: When and where did Moses live?
Circle every time expression and put it on the board timeline.
Two colors: What the Children of Israel believed / what the Pharaoh believed about himself.
Draw arrows: The Pharaoh’s fear → rude and harsh → dangerous work for little or no money.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the fear-to-action chain in view.
Language Focus: Sort the time expressions (Activity 1), rewrite the fear and the forced work (Activity 2), then choose So / That’s why / to rule (Activity 3).
Write five connected sentences about another historical situation (Activity 4).
Name one fair alternative a ruler could choose instead of acting from fear.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Timeline hook: Learners guess how long ago the story happened and write the guess on the board line; 5–13 Listen with books closed (when and where?), then read along and circle every time expression; 13–20 Pairs build a two-row chain on paper (beliefs / the Pharaoh’s fear → harsh treatment → forced work), each arrow with a quoted phrase, quick whole-class check; 20–24 Quick Challenge individually; 24–32 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (When in history? When does time jump?), then the “Did it happen?” question on the board before Activities 2–3 in pairs; 32–38 Use: Pairs choose a period they studied in history class and draft five sentences (At that time …, people feared that … would …, That’s why …), two pairs read aloud and the class names the result sentence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which sentence tells us what the Pharaoh believed about himself, and why is that not the narrator’s view?
Why did the Children of Israel not believe that the Pharaoh was a god?
What did the Pharaoh’s fear lead him to do, and what would a fair ruler do instead?

Replay the fear sentence and ask learners to raise a hand when they hear “would”.
Use the audio and image to set the scene only; do not add dates or historical details that are not in the chapter.

differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six connected sentences about a different historical situation using a time frame, “feared that … would …”, “That’s why …” and one passive sentence with “were made to”.

formativeAssessment: Attributes the Pharaoh’s self-image to him, not to the narrator.
Builds the fear → decision → result chain with evidence.
Uses “would” after a past verb and a result linker correctly.
expectedResponses: The Pharaoh feared that the Children of Israel, a group larger than the Egyptians, would take control of his kingdom. That’s why he was harsh to them and made them do dangerous work for little or no money.
content.transferTask: Describe a fear-based decision in a neutral setting (a club, a class, a team) and propose a fairer alternative in two sentences.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover “would” as a future seen from the past before I named it, and did they keep the Pharaoh’s fear as a reason rather than an excuse?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, build a two-row chain on paper: beliefs, the Pharaoh’s fear, harsh treatment, forced work. Put a quoted phrase on every arrow.

interculturalFocus.notice: The chapter places the story in the 13th century BC, over 3000 years ago, and says the Pharaoh 'saw himself as a god'.

interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners separate the ruler from the people of Egypt. Ancient Egypt also gave the world writing, medicine and astronomy; the chapter judges one ruler's actions.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write key words in each box.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads up to “a god” and B reads the rest. Each explains the main idea to the partner without looking. The partner asks one question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about the family of the Israelites. Asker asks “Who was their grandfather?”. Writer draws a simple family tree. Change roles for the sentences about the Pharaoh.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: An exchange student asks, “What makes a ruler fair?” The learner gives two ideas and compares them with the Pharaoh.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “He used every method to upset them.” into their home language. Which word did each pair choose for “method”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why the Pharaoh feared the Children of Israel. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter ends with the Pharaoh’s dream. Why does the writer stop here?” (We want to know what the dream means.)

thinkAloud.sentence: That’s why he was rude and harsh to the Children of Israel.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “That’s why” points back to the sentence before. The Pharaoh feared that this large group would take control of his kingdom. That is the reason for his cruelty. Learners find one more reason in the chapter and say it with “because”.

stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What did the Pharaoh believe about himself?

onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate one question about the Pharaoh’s dream.

objectives: Keep four kinds of information apart: The dream (reported by Ibn Abbas), the advisors’ prediction, the Pharaoh’s order and the mother’s fear.
Explain how a prediction becomes a harmful decision and then fear inside one family, without graphic detail.

Discover “will” for a prediction (will be born, will die), sequence with When / Then, and describe a strong feeling and its result (so frightened that, was scared that … could, did not know what to do).
Recognize the human impact of decisions that target innocent people.
content.pedagogy: Use four cards on the board: Dream / Prediction / Order / Family. Learners place each key sentence under a card while listening, so reported information never turns into narrator fact. The killing of babies is read once, calmly, by the teacher or the audio and is never acted out; attention moves quickly to the mother. Grammar is discovered from function: You ask “Are the advisors telling us something that happened?” and learners find that “will” predicts.
priorKnowledge: Past simple narrative, “when” clauses and simple imperatives (Sit down. Open your books.).
anticipatedMisconceptions: The advisors’ words are a prediction reported inside the story, not narrator commentary. The chapter gives two descriptions of the dream (the throne in Chapter 1, the fire here from Ibn Abbas); keep both attributed and do not merge or explain them.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: will + base verb for a prediction, including the passive “will be born” · When + past simple / Then for sequence · the imperative with no subject (Kill …, Take a basket.) · so + adjective + that + result · was scared that … could (can moves back after a past verb) · question word + to + verb (what to do).
Notice (Activity 1): board “A boy will be born of the Children of Israel …”. Ask: “Has this happened yet? What are the advisors doing?” Learners decide it is a prediction and explain why “will be born” (not “will born”).
Build (Activities 2–3): put the events in order with When / Then, then correct such → so, can → could and what doing → what to do. After each correction ask: “What does the new form tell us about the mother?”
Likely errors: *will born · *such frightened that · *she was scared that the soldiers can hear · *She did not know what doing / what to do she.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a safe situation in which someone receives a warning and must decide what to do (a storm warning, a lost ticket before a trip).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrast three voices: calm reporting (“Ibn ABbas SAID, | …”), prediction with a steady fall (“a BOY will be BORN | …”) and the short order, read flat and quickly, never performed.
Feeling + result: stress the degree word and pause before “that”: “She was SO FRIGHTened | that she was unABLE to SLEEP at NIGHT.”
Weak forms: “was” /wəz/ and “that” /ðət/ in “was SCARED that | when MOses CRIED …”.
Word focus: ad-VI-sors, ma-GI-cians, je-RU-sa-lem, NEW-born, HEART-less, FRIGHT-ened (two syllables, /nd/).
beforeReading: Show the four cards (Dream / Prediction / Order / Family). Ask pairs: “Why is a dream not the same as a fact? Why is a prediction not the same as an order?” Collect two answers.
duringReading: First listening: Which card does each sentence belong to? Learners point to the card.
Underline the two “will” forms in the advisors’ words.
Mark “When he woke up” and “Then”.
Underline three phrases that show the mother’s fear and one action she takes (She prayed to Allah for help).
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge using the four cards.
Language Focus: Discover “will” for prediction (Activity 1), order the events with When / Then (Activity 2), correct so / could / what to do (Activity 3).
Write five connected sentences about a warning and a response in a safe setting (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Four-card hook: Dream / Prediction / Order / Family on the board, pairs explain why a dream is not a fact; 5–12 Listen once (the teacher reads the soldiers’ sentences calmly), learners point to the right card for each sentence; 12–19 Read in pairs and fill a four-column table with one quoted phrase per column, then find the three fear phrases and the mother’s action; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Has this happened yet?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then two pairs explain one correction each; 31–38 Use: A safe warning story in five sentences (They said that … will …, a short order, so … that …, did not know what to do, asked for help), partners check the “so … that” sentence; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Who reports the dream, and who makes the prediction?
At what moment does a prediction become an order?
Which sentence shows most clearly how the order affected one family?
interactiveTips: Use The Dream hotspot for the report and the prediction, and the A Mother’s Prayer hotspot for her fear and prayer.
Pause the audio at each change of speaker and ask “Whose words are these?”
Do not role-play, draw or discuss details of the soldiers’ actions; move from the order straight to the mother.

content.transferTask: Describe a safe warning situation: What someone predicted, what instruction followed, how people felt and one responsible next action.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep dream, prediction and order apart, and did the lesson stay calm and non-graphic while still showing the family’s fear?

How many phrases per column? (one)

content.chapter: Chapter 3: A Baby in the River
objectives: Trace the route instruction → action → river → palace → Asiye’s decision with evidence.
Explain how worry and trust exist together in Moses’s mother (so sad, but she knew …).
Discover why the chapter says “The basket was carried away by the waters” (passive focus) and use but / also / while + -ing / Soon and a who-clause between commas.
Describe protective action by several people, including Asiye’s decision with “will”.
content.pedagogy: Turn the chapter into a route map with four stops (home → river → shore near the palace → the queen). A learner moves a marker from stop to stop while the audio plays; the class says who or what is acting at each stop. When the basket leaves the mother’s hands, ask “Who is the story following now?” Learners discover that the passive puts the basket first because the basket is now the center of the story.
priorKnowledge: Imperatives, past simple and “but” for contrast; recognition of was + past participle.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Trust is not passive waiting: The mother acts, sends her daughter to follow the basket and still feels sad. Queen Asiye is described as different from her husband; learners should not assume that everyone in the palace agreed with the Pharaoh.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: passive was + past participle + by to keep the focus on the basket (The basket was carried away by the waters) · but (contrast), also (adding), while + -ing (two things at the same time), Soon (moving on) · a who-clause between commas that adds information about a person (The queen, who was different from her husband, was …) · will for a decision (I will take him …) · imperatives (Put …, Take …).
Notice (Activity 1): board “There she put the basket in the water. The basket was carried away by the waters.” Ask: “Who is the subject in the first sentence? And in the second? Why does the writer change?” Learners find that the story now follows the basket.
Build (Activities 2–3): Fill in but / also / while / Soon and explain why “during” and “so” do not fit, then rebuild the who-sentence and say where the extra information sits.
Likely errors: *The basket carried away (no was) · *during carrying · *The queen, who was different from her husband, she was good (extra pronoun) · *I take him (no will for a decision).
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a person who receives guidance, feels worried and then makes a decision.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Instructions: short falling units, “PUT your BAby in the BASket. | TAKE the BASket to the RIVer NILE.”
Passive: “was” is weak and the past participle is stressed: “The BASket was (/wəz/) CARried aWAY | by the WAters.” -ed in carried /d/.
Contrast: pause before “but”: “She was SO SAD, | but she KNEW …”.
Relative clause: lower the voice slightly between the commas: “The QUEEN, | who was DIFferent from her HUSband, | was GOOD …”.
Word focus: SHEL-ter, a-SHORE, SER-vants, kind-HEART-ed, PAL-ace.
beforeReading: Draw four stops on the board (home / river / shore near the palace / the queen). Ask: “Who might act at each stop?” Accept predictions without confirming them.
duringReading: A volunteer moves a marker along the four stops during the audio.
Underline the passive sentence about the basket.
Mark one sentence of worry and one of trust in the second part.
Box Asiye’s decision with “will”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the route map in view.
Language Focus: Discover the passive focus (Activity 1), complete the contrast-addition-time lines (Activity 2), rebuild the who-sentence (Activity 3).
Write five sentences about guidance, worry and a decision (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Route hook: Four stops on the board, pairs predict who acts at each stop; 4–12 Listen while a volunteer moves a marker along the route, then read along; 12–19 Actor or object? Pairs list who or what is the subject at each stop (the mother, the basket, the waves, the servants, the queen) and quote one sentence each; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Why does the subject change to “the basket”?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners explain why “during” does not fit; 31–38 Use: Think-pair-share, learners tell a partner about a time they received advice and felt worried, then write five sentences with but, while and will, and one partner reads theirs aloud; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the second sentence start with “The basket” and not with the mother?
Which words show that the mother was sad and trusting at the same time?
What information about Queen Asiye prepares us for her decision?

Replay the two sentences about the basket back to back and ask what changed in the subject.
Keep the image to what the text states; do not add details about the river journey.

objectives: Give the three women their own role: The queen asks for a nurse, the sister acts immediately, the mother becomes the nurse.
Explain the problem–solution chain that brings Moses back to his mother and the later change over time.
Understand words of care and belonging (immediately, nearby, raised him, felt close to, originally) and choose to + verb (purpose), because of + noun and because + clause (reason).
Correct will be, became and willing to help, and connect helpfulness with a lasting quality.
content.pedagogy: Use a cooperation map: Three columns (Queen Asiye / Moses’s sister / Moses’s mother) and, under them, a growth line (baby → grew up safely → became a strong young man). Learners fill the columns from the text before any value is named. For language, you ask “Why did she bring her mother?” and “Why do people remember Asiye?” and learners discover that the first answer is a purpose (to be) and the second a reason (because of + noun).
priorKnowledge: “Because”, “to + verb” for purpose, and past forms of common irregular verbs (become → became, grow → grew).
anticipatedMisconceptions: The outcome is not the work of one person; the chapter gives each woman a distinct action. Moses grows up in the palace but the chapter says he knew that the Pharaoh was not a god and felt close to the Children of Israel.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: meaning of care and belonging words (immediately, nearby, raised him, felt close to, originally) · to + base verb for purpose (to be Moses’s nurse) · because of + noun phrase vs because + clause · will + base verb (She will be a good nurse) · became for a change of state · willing to + base verb with always for a lasting quality.
Notice (Activity 1): learners match five words with meanings, then say which words describe how fast the sister acted and where Moses felt he belonged.
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete to / because of / because and explain why “for be” is impossible, then correct will is, become and willing helping. Ask: “Which answer tells us WHY she did it, which one tells us WHAT FOR?”
Likely errors: *for be · *because of she was good · *She will is · *Moses become (past) · *willing helping.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a person who receives help, grows over time and develops responsibility or a sense of belonging.
content.pronunciationFocus:
The sister’s speech as three short units, with a confident fall on the prediction: “I KNOW a good WOman. | She LIVES nearBY. | She will BE a GOOD NURSE for the BAby.” (“will” stays clear here: /wɪl/).
Stress the time shift: “YEARS PASSED | and MOses beCAME | a STRONG YOUNG MAN.”
Weak forms: “to” /tə/ in “to BE Moses’s NURSE” and “willing to HELP”.
Word focus: im-ME-di-ate-ly, o-RIG-i-nal-ly, COUR-age, pro-TEC-tor, near-BY.

duringReading: Fill the three columns with one action and one quoted phrase each.
Underline “to be Moses’s nurse” and “because of her goodness and courage”.
Build the growth line: Grew up safely → became a strong young man → always willing to help.
Find the reason Moses felt close to the Children of Israel.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the cooperation map.
Language Focus: Match the care and belonging words (Activity 1), choose purpose or reason (Activity 2), correct will be / became / willing to help (Activity 3).
Write five sentences about a person who grows into a role (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: Three names on the board, pairs pencil in one predicted action for each; 5–12 Listen and read, then correct the pencil predictions with the text; 12–19 Cooperation map in groups of three: Each learner becomes the “expert” on one woman, finds her action and a quoted phrase and reports it to the group, then the group adds the growth line; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs, Activity 2 as whole-class discovery (WHY or WHAT FOR?), Activity 3 individually with pair check; 31–38 Use: Learners write five sentences about someone who helped them grow (a coach, an older sibling, a teacher) with to + verb, because / because of and became, then swap and underline the reason and the purpose; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does each of the three women do, and why do all three actions matter?
Why do people always remember Queen Asiye, according to the chapter?
Why did Moses feel close to the Children of Israel although he grew up in the palace?
interactiveTips: Use The Nurse hotspot for the return and the A Loving Home hotspot for raising him and her goodness and courage.
Pause at “Years passed” and ask learners to move to the growth line.
Ask for the exact sentence before an action is written in a column.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give three actor cards and the frames “She brought her mother to ____.”, “People remember her because of ____.” and “Moses became ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six connected sentences combining the three women’s roles with one purpose, one because of, one because-clause and one change with became.

formativeAssessment: Assigns each action to the right person.
Distinguishes purpose (to be) from reason (because of / because).
Uses will be, became and willing to + verb accurately.
expectedResponses: Moses’s sister ran to the queen and brought her mother to be his nurse, so Moses was in his mother’s arms again. Queen Asiye raised him with love. He grew up safely, became a strong young man, was always willing to help the weak and felt close to the Children of Israel because his mother was one of them.
content.transferTask: Explain how several people helped one person grow, using one purpose (to + verb), one reason (because / because of) and one change (became).
content.teacherReflection: Did every woman keep her own role on the map, and could learners say whether an answer gave a reason or a purpose?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups of three, each learner is the expert on one woman. Find her action and a quoted phrase and report it to the group. Then add the growth line together.
checkQuestions: How many women? (three, one each)
What do you report? (her action and a quote)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the sister, the mother and Queen Asiye each have the right action. In Activity 2, listen for WHY or WHAT FOR. In the Use task, ask partners to underline the reason and the purpose.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “to + verb” (purpose) and one with “because of + noun” (reason) about someone who helped you.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives each action to the right person.
rubricLevels.notYet: Read one action and ask “Who did this?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells purpose (to be) from reason (because).
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Why, or what for?”.

rubricLevels.notYet: Give one model of each.

interculturalFocus.notice: Three women act together to protect Moses: the queen, his sister and his mother.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Who helps raise a child in a Turkish family (grandmothers, aunts, neighbours)? Is it similar in English-speaking families, or do nurseries and childminders play a bigger role? What does the saying 'It takes a village to raise a child' mean?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners describe different family models without saying one is better. Some learners may live in non-traditional families; keep the talk general.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note the sister’s plan and young Moses.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain in two sentences why young Moses felt close to the Israelites.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner how Moses’s sister helped. The partner says why her plan was clever.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Questioner asks “Why do people remember Queen Asiye?”. Finder reads the answer sentence. Summarizer says it in his or her own words.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Which brave woman from history do people in your country remember?” The learner names one and compares her with Queen Asiye.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “People always remember her because of her goodness and courage.” into their home language. Which words did each pair choose for “goodness” and “courage”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Moses’s sister brought her mother to the palace. Next lesson ask what their listener said about the sister.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer says ‘Allah is the Best Protector.’ Why does this short sentence come after the mother gets her baby back?” (It explains what happened.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The explanation gives the reason with “because”. The notes name Queen Asiye.

thinkAloud.sentence: She said to her servants, “Find a nurse for the baby.”
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The queen needs a nurse, and Moses’s sister saw everything. I think the sister will bring their mother to the palace. Learners make their own guess, then read on and check it.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “raised him in the palace with love.”

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: What was young Moses like?

content.chapter: Chapter 5: A Mistake in the Bazaar
objectives: Separate background, sudden call for help, action, unintended result and Moses’s response on Day 1 from the new situation on Day 2.
Explain that the death was accidental and that Moses still admitted his mistake and asked for forgiveness.
Discover while + past continuous for an action in progress, and use saw, who-clauses and “understood that” for a conclusion.
Recognize what short spoken lines do: Call for help, ask for forgiveness, admit a mistake, accuse with a question.
content.pedagogy: Draw a vertical line on the board: Day 1 | Day 2. Learners place each event on the correct side, so the first day’s accident and the next day’s accusation never merge. The death is stated once, factually, and never dramatised; the lesson centers on responsibility. For language, you ask “Did Moses finish his walk before he saw the fight?” and learners discover that “was walking” is the background already in progress.
priorKnowledge: Past simple and past continuous forms; “who” for people.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Accidentally” does not mean “without consequences”: Moses is very upset, says “I have wronged myself” and asks for forgiveness. Moses’s prayer comes from the Qur’an (Surah al-Qasas: 15–16); it is read and understood, never gapped or rewritten.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: while + past continuous for the background vs past simple for the event (while Moses was walking …, he saw …) · Suddenly for a new, unexpected action · saw for a single finished event · who-clause for a person (the same man … who Moses helped the day before) · understood that + conclusion · what short spoken lines do: Imperatives (Help me!), present perfect to admit (I have wronged myself), be going to as an accusing question.
Notice (Activity 1): Read “One day, while Moses (pbuh) was walking in the bazaar, he saw two men fighting.” Ask: “Was the walk finished when he saw the fight? Which action is longer?” Learners draw a long line (walking) and a short mark (saw) before you name the forms.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose saw / who / that for the next day, then match each spoken line with what the speaker is doing.
Likely errors: *while Moses walked (losing the background) · *was seeing · which for a person · *understood what · *I have wronged myself yesterday.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a tense but safe public situation (a queue, a crowded bus stop) with while …, suddenly, a who-clause and “understood that …”.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Background then event, with a pause at the comma: “One DAY, | while MOses was WALKing in the baZAAR, | he SAW two MEN FIGHTing.”
Contrastive stress in the admission: “I DIDn’t do it on PURpose.” / “I have WRONGED mySELF.” (wronged /d/). Read the prayer calmly, not theatrically.
Accusing question: A falling tone on “Are you GOing to KILL me TOO?” shows it is not a real question; read it once, neutrally, without acting.
Word focus: ba-ZAAR, ac-ci-DEN-tal-ly, QUAR-rel-some, PEACE-a-ble, PAR-doned (/d/).
beforeReading: Give a harmless classroom example: “While Ali was carrying a tray of glasses, someone opened the door and the glasses broke.” Ask: “Did Ali mean to break them? What should he do now?” Introduce the words intention and consequence.
duringReading: Divide the page: Day 1 / Day 2.
On Day 1 mark background (was walking), sudden event (Suddenly …), action, result and Moses’s response.
Underline the three sentences of Moses’s prayer and label them: ask / explain / admit.
On Day 2 find the sentence with “understood that” and the evidence that led to it.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the two-day line.
Language Focus: discover while + past continuous (Activity 1), choose saw / who / that (Activity 2), match the spoken lines with their functions (Activity 3).
Write five sentences about a tense public situation (Activity 4).
Name one honest response after an unintended mistake: admit, apologize, repair.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: The harmless “tray of glasses” example, learners separate intention and consequence; 5–12 Listen with books closed (what happened on each day?), then read along; 12–19 Two-day line in pairs: Day 1 background / event / result / response and Day 2 evidence / conclusion, each with a quoted phrase, whole-class check at the board; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery with the long line and short mark on the board, Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 as a card sort (speech line / function) in pairs; 31–38 Use: Learners write a five-sentence mini-narrative about a tense but safe public moment, then partners check that the while-sentence uses the past continuous; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which words tell us the death was not intended?
What does Moses do after the mistake, and what does this show about responsibility?
What evidence helps Moses understand that the man is quarrelsome on the second day?
interactiveTips: Use The Mistake hotspot for the Day 1 sequence and the Forgiveness hotspot for Moses’s prayer and Allah’s pardon.
Replay the first sentence and ask learners to draw the long line and the short mark as they listen.
Do not replay the fight for effect or act out any part of it.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give five boxes (background / sudden event / result / response / next day) and the frames “While ____ was ____ing, ____.” and “He understood that ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences about a safe situation that separate intention from consequence, include an honest admission with the present perfect and end with a conclusion using “understood that”.

formativeAssessment: Keeps Day 1 and Day 2 separate.
Uses while + past continuous for background and past simple for the event.
Explains what each spoken line does (ask, admit, accuse).
expectedResponses: While Moses was walking in the bazaar, he saw two men fighting and helped the weak man, but he accidentally caused the Egyptian’s death. He was very upset, admitted his mistake and asked Allah for forgiveness, and Allah pardoned him. The next day he understood that the Israelite was a quarrelsome man.
content.transferTask: Describe a safe, unintended mistake in five steps: background → event → consequence → honest response → lesson.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discuss responsibility calmly without dramatising the death, and did they discover the background role of “was walking” themselves?

classroomManagement.instructions: In pairs, draw a two-day line. For Day 1 write background, event, result and response. For Day 2 write evidence and conclusion. Add a quoted phrase to each.
checkQuestions: How many days? (two)
What goes on Day 2? (evidence and conclusion)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Keep the tone calm. Check that “accidentally” is on Day 1 as the result. In Activity 1, use the long line and short mark on the board. In the Use task, check the past continuous after while.

exitTicket: Write one “while … was …ing, … ” sentence about your morning and one honest sentence you could say after a mistake.

rubricLevels.notYet: Give the two day headings.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates what he intended from what happened.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Did he plan it?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses while + past continuous for background and past simple for the event.
rubricLevels.notYet: Draw the long line and short mark.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes an honest response to a mistake.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to “admitted his mistake”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Moses helps a man in the bazaar, and the death is accidental. Moses admits his mistake and asks for forgiveness.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: In English law there is a difference between an accident and a crime ('accidental', 'intentional'). Is there the same difference in Turkish ('kaza ile', 'kasıtlı')? Why do many cultures make this difference?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners keep the chapter's distinction and talk about responsibility, not punishment.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note the two days in the bazaar. Keep the tone calm.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners compare the two days in two sentences with “The next day”.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner what Moses understood on the second day. The partner gives the word from the book.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Finder finds the sentence with “quarrelsome”. Reader reads it aloud. Explainer explains the difference between quarrelsome and peaceable.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “What should you do when a friend always starts fights?” The learner answers and links it to the second day.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Moses was very upset.” into their home language. Which word did each pair choose for “upset”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what happened in the bazaar on the second day. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter ends with a question from the Israelite. Why does the writer end with his words?” (They show the danger for Moses.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The retell is calm. Learners say that the first day was an accident.

thinkAloud.sentence: The man once more called out to Moses, “Help me!”
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: Who is “The man”? The sentence before says it was the same man from the Children of Israel whom Moses helped the day before. Learners find one more he, she or they and say who it is.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “This is of Satan’s doing.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What did Moses say to Allah after his mistake?

onlineTask.reply: Write one sentence about why saying sorry is important.

objectives: Distinguish the danger already happening (are looking for you) from the expected next event (are going to catch you).
Explain why Moses leaves Egypt and why Midian matters (The Pharaoh was not the ruler in this land).
Follow the move from warning to journey to a new scene at the well, including the girls’ unusual behavior.
Use be going to, a chain of past simple verbs, where / who clauses and question word order (Why are you sitting …?).
content.pedagogy: Teach the chapter as a scene change: NOW (danger) → NEXT (expected capture) → GO (urgent advice) → JOURNEY → NEW PLACE. Learners hold up NOW / NEXT cards while the man’s warning is replayed. For language, you ask “How does the man know the soldiers will catch him?” and learners discover that “are going to” is a prediction based on what is happening now.
priorKnowledge: Present continuous, be going to for plans and imperatives.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Midian matters because the Pharaoh was not the ruler there, not only because it is far away. The chapter also says Moses was not alone “as Allah guided him”; he still arrived tired and thirsty.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be going to for a prediction based on present evidence (are looking for you → are going to catch you) · urgent imperative (Run away from the city.) · knew that + reason · a chain of past simple verbs (escaped, left, traveled) and After many days · past continuous for what someone was doing when a new scene begins · where for a place and who for people · question word order (Why are you sitting …? Why aren’t you taking …?).
Notice (Activity 1): board “The Pharaoh’s soldiers are looking for you. … Now they are going to catch you.” Ask: “Is the search happening now? How does the man know what will happen next?”
Build (Activities 2–3): order the journey sentences and name the signal words, then correct which → where, which → who and “Why you are sitting”.
Likely errors: *Why you are sitting …? · *a well which many men gathered · *shepherds which were watering · *They are going to catching you.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about someone who must leave a place quickly and arrives somewhere unfamiliar, ending with a “Why are you …?” question.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrast now and next with stress: “The SOLdiers are LOOKing for you. | NOW they are GOing to CATCH you.” In fast speech “going to” may sound like /ˈɡənə/; learners should recognize it but write “going to”.
Urgent imperative with a firm fall: “RUN aWAY from the CIty.”
-ed endings in the journey chain: escaped /t/, traveled /d/, reached /t/, gathered /d/.
Questions: Falling tone on Wh-questions, “WHY are you SITting far aWAY from the SPRING?”
Word focus: PUN-ish-ment, MID-i-an, SHEP-herds (silent h), CAT-tle, WA-ter-ing.
beforeReading: Write NOW and NEXT on two cards. Give two neutral sentences (Dark clouds are coming. It is going to rain.) and ask which card fits each and how we know.
duringReading: Hold up NOW or NEXT when you hear the man’s warning.
Number the journey verbs: escaped → left → traveled → reached.
Underline the sentence that explains why Midian is safer.
Mark what is unusual about the two girls at the well.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge using the scene-change map.
Language Focus: Discover “are going to” from present evidence (Activity 1), order the journey (Activity 2), correct where / who / the question (Activity 3).
Write five sentences about leaving quickly and arriving somewhere new (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 NOW / NEXT hook with the rain example; 4–11 Listen while learners hold up NOW or NEXT at the warning, then read along; 11–18 Scene-change map in pairs: Five boxes (danger / expected capture / advice / journey / new place) with a quoted phrase each, then the class explains why Midian matters; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (How does the man know?), Activity 2 in pairs naming the signal words, Activity 3 individually with pair check; 30–37 Use: Pairs draft a five-sentence mini-narrative about a traveler who must leave early because of a storm and arrives in an unknown town, ending with a Why-question to a stranger, then two pairs read and the class checks the question word order; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What danger is already happening, and what is expected to happen next?
Why does the chapter tell us that the Pharaoh was not the ruler in Midian?
What does Moses notice at the well that makes him ask a question?
interactiveTips: Use the A Warning hotspot for the warning and the journey, and The Well in Midian hotspot for the new scene.
Replay the warning and let learners raise NOW / NEXT cards.
Pause before Moses’s questions to mark the start of a new scene.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames “They are ____ing. They are going to ____. ____ (order)! After many days, he ____.” and one model Why-question.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write seven connected sentences moving from present danger to a new place, with one where-clause, one who-clause and two correct Why-questions.

formativeAssessment: Distinguishes present danger from expected consequence.
Explains why Midian is safer, using the chapter sentence.
Uses where / who and Wh-question word order correctly.
expectedResponses: A man from the city warned Moses that the soldiers were looking for him and were going to catch him, so he left Egypt. After many days he reached Midian, where the Pharaoh was not the ruler, and at the well he asked two girls why they were sitting far away from the spring.
content.transferTask: Write five sentences about someone who leaves quickly because of a present danger and asks a polite question in a new place.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners discover that “are going to” rests on present evidence, and did they see that the chapter ends by opening a new situation?

classroomManagement.instructions: Hold up NOW or NEXT when you hear the warning. Then, in pairs, fill five boxes: danger, expected capture, advice, journey, new place. Add a quoted phrase to each.
checkQuestions: What do you hold up? (NOW or NEXT)
How many boxes? (five)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Watch the NOW and NEXT cards during listening. Check that pairs explain why Midian is safer with the chapter sentence. In the Use task, check the word order of the Why-question.

rubric: Reason for leaving and safety of Midian
exitTicket: Write one present-continuous sentence about something happening now and one “going to” prediction based on it.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells present danger from expected consequence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is this happening now, or next?”.

rubricLevels.criterion: Reason for leaving and safety of Midian
rubricLevels.secure: Explains why he left and why Midian is safer.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the sentence about the ruler.

rubricLevels.secure: Orders the scenes.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the five box headings.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses where, who and Wh-question word order.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write the question from the text as a model.

interculturalFocus.notice: Moses leaves Egypt for Midian, where the Pharaoh does not rule. Crossing a border can mean safety.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which English words describe people who leave their country to be safe ('refugee', 'asylum')? Which Turkish words are used (mülteci, sığınmacı)? Why is careful language important here?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Some learners may have family histories of migration. Speak about people who move with dignity, and never ask anyone to share their story.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note the warning, the journey and the well.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain in three sentences how Moses reached Midian.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner where Midian was. The partner explains why it was a safe place for Moses.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentences about the well. Listener notes who was there. Writer writes Moses’s two questions.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Where do people meet in a village in your country?” The learner answers and compares it with the well in Midian.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “He was not alone as Allah guided him.” into their home language. How did each pair translate “as” here?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why Moses left Egypt and where he went. Next lesson ask what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer says ‘The Pharaoh was not the ruler in this land.’ Why is this sentence important?” (It shows that Moses was safe.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The steps are in the right order. The retell names Midian and the well.

thinkAloud.sentence: Moses escaped from the soldiers.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: I want to sum up this chapter. A man warned Moses, he left Egypt, and after many days he came to a well in Midian. My sentence is: Moses ran away from Egypt and found a new land where the Pharaoh did not rule. Learners sum up the next paragraph in one sentence.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Run away from the city.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What did the man from the far end of the city tell Moses?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences about the well in Midian.
onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate why the girls did not go near the spring.

objectives: Infer the sisters’ need from their own explanation before naming helpfulness.
Explain how Moses’s action changes their routine (they come home early).
Discover the meaning of “did not have to” (not necessary, not “not allowed”) and use cannot, So, have to and until.
Rephrase a result as a reason (That’s why → because / as / since) and “there are no …” as “do not have any …”.
content.pedagogy: Use a before-help / after-help table. Learners fill the “before” column only from the sisters’ own words (limitation → obligation → waiting), then the “after” column from the conversation with their father. The discovery question is the father’s surprise: “You came home very early! Why?” Learners find that “We did not have to wait” means the waiting was no longer necessary.
priorKnowledge: Can / cannot, have to, “until” with time (until 5 o’clock).
anticipatedMisconceptions: Turkish learners often read “did not have to” as “were not allowed to” (izin yoktu); in the chapter it means “there was no need” (gerek yoktu). The help is based on a need stated in the dialogue, not on how the sisters look.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: did not have to = not necessary (not “must not”) · cannot for inability · So for a result · have to for necessity · until + clause for the end point of waiting (present simple after until: until the other shepherds go away) · That’s why (result) vs because / as / since (reason) · there are no … = do not have any ….
Notice (Activity 1): board “We did not have to wait until the other shepherds went away.” Ask: “Were they forbidden to wait, or was waiting not necessary? What changed?” Learners decide before seeing the options.
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete cannot / So / until and explain why “must not” and “during” do not fit, then turn “That’s why” into “because / as / since” and “There are no young men” into “We do not have any young men”.
Likely errors: did not have to read as “not allowed” · *He must not come (for cannot) · *until the other shepherds will go away · *We do not have no young men.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about people who usually have to do something difficult but receive unexpected help one day.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the sisters’ explanation and stress the obligation: “So, | we HAVE to TAKE the SHEEP to the WAter ourSELVES.” In “have to” the v sounds like /f/: /ˈhæf tə/.
Contrastive stress on the change: “We DIDN’T HAVE to WAIT.”
“cannot” keeps its stress: “He CANnot COME with us.” Contrast with weak “can” /kən/.
Word focus: SHEP-herds (silent h), MES-sen-ger, PA-tient (/ʃ/), AK-a-ba, EAR-ly.
beforeReading: Ask: “How can we know that someone needs help? From how they look, or from what they say?” Collect ideas and keep the question on the board.
duringReading: Underline every reason the sisters give (father very old / no young men).
Circle “have to” and “until”.
Mark what Moses does in one sentence.
Find the father’s surprise and the sisters’ answer with “did not have to”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the before/after table.
Language Focus: Discover “did not have to” (Activity 1), complete cannot / So / until (Activity 2), rephrase reason and “there are no” (Activity 3).
Write five sentences about a routine that changes after unexpected help (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: “How can we know someone needs help?” two answers on the board; 5–12 Listen and read, pairs answer the board question from the text; 12–19 Before/after table in pairs: Before help (cannot → have to → until) and after help (came home early, did not have to wait), every cell with a quoted phrase; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (forbidden or not necessary?), then a quick Turkish check (gerek yoktu / izin yoktu), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–38 Use: Learners describe a school routine (waiting for the photocopier, carrying chairs after an event) that changed when someone helped, five sentences with have to, until and did not have to, then one partner reads theirs aloud; 38–40 Exit ticket.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: A Simple Life in Midian
objectives: Explain why Moses accepts the job (a stranger who urgently needed a job and a house) and what the years in Midian contain.
Follow the long stable period → decision to return → winter journey → sudden fire.
Discover the difference between background sentences (It was winter. It was getting dark and cold. They were crossing a valley.) and main events (took, started, saw, said).
Rephrase time, result and purpose (After living … → After he had lived …, because → so, to get warm → so that we can get warm).
content.pedagogy: Draw a long horizontal timeline: Ten years in Midian as a wide bar, then the journey as a short bar that ends with a sudden mark (the fire). Learners place work, marriage and the simple, patient life on the long bar, so the years are not an empty gap. Then they sort the last paragraph into “scene” and “action” sentences and discover that the background is built with “was” and the past continuous before “Suddenly” breaks in.
priorKnowledge: Past simple and past continuous; “after + time”; purpose with to + verb.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The years in Midian are not empty waiting: Moses works, marries and lives a simple life with patience. The decision to return is made “with the guidance of Allah”. The fire is only what Moses sees; learners should not add explanations that come in the next chapter.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: background (It was + noun/adjective, past continuous: was getting dark, were crossing) vs main events in the past simple (took, started, saw, said) · Suddenly for an event that breaks into the background · meaning of situation words (a stranger, urgently, with patience, hillside, burning sticks) · After + -ing = After + subject + had lived · because (reason) → so (result) · to + verb = so that + subject + can (purpose).
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six parts of the last paragraph. Ask: “Which sentences only describe the scene? Which ones make the story move?” Then: “What does ‘Suddenly’ do to the scene?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Match the situation words, then rewrite After living / because / to get warm with the new structures.
Likely errors: *After lived in Midian · *Suddenly Moses was seeing a fire · *so that we get warm (missing can) · *He was a stranger because he accepted the offer (reversing reason and result).
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about someone who spends a long time in one place, decides to leave and changes action because of a sudden situation.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the long opening: “AFter LIVing in MIDian | for aBOUT TEN YEARS, | with the GUIDance of alLAH, | MOses deCIDed | to GO BACK to EGypt.”
Read the background slowly and evenly, then pause before the event: “It was GETting DARK and COLD. | They were CROSSing a VALley … | SUDdenly, | MOses SAW a FIRE.”
-ed endings: accepted /ɪd/, needed /ɪd/, helped /t/, married /d/, traveled /d/.
Word focus: STRAN-ger, UR-gent-ly, PA-tience (/ʃ/), VAL-ley, HILL-side.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can a quiet period in someone’s life still be important? What could happen in ten quiet years?” Pairs list two ideas.
duringReading: Underline the reason Moses accepts the offer.

Circle “decided to” and “started to”.
Box “Suddenly” and draw a line between the scene and the event.

Write five sentences about a change of plan (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “What could happen in ten quiet years?” two ideas per pair; 4–11 Listen and read, learners stop the audio at “Suddenly” and predict nothing beyond what Moses says; 11–18 Long timeline on the board: Volunteers place the job offer, work, marriage, the patient life, the decision, the journey and the fire, each with a quoted phrase; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as a card sort in pairs followed by the whole-class question (What does Suddenly do?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 individually with pair check; 30–37 Use: Each learner writes a five-sentence change-of-plan story (After working …, decided to …, It was …, was …ing, Suddenly …, to + verb), a partner underlines the background sentences in one color and the events in another; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did Moses accept the job, according to the chapter?
What shows that the years in Midian were a meaningful stage?
Which sentences build the winter scene, and which word changes it?

content.chapter: Chapter 9: The Voice on the Mountain
objectives: Trace each command to Moses’s action and its result (put down → turned into a big snake, put your hand … → shining like silver).
Separate the two signs from the mission reported later (go to Egypt, show the Pharaoh the signs, warn him).
Explain the new role marked by “became” and the response marked by “Upon this”.
Use turn into, tell + person + to + verb, became and Then / Once more in connected B1 production.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is sacred and dense, so it is taught in two lessons. Lesson 1 builds two command → action → result chains and marks where the mission begins; Allah’s words are heard from the audio or read by the teacher once, calmly, and never performed, gapped or rewritten by learners. Lesson 2 opens the language: Learners discover that “Upon this” links the message with Moses’s immediate response, that “told Moses to go” reports the mission without quoting it, and that “became” marks the new role.
priorKnowledge: Imperatives, past simple of common verbs, and “become”.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Upon this” does not mean “on top of the mountain”. The signs belong to a mission (show these signs to the Pharaoh); they are not tricks. Do not add details about the mountain or the voice that are not in the text.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: Upon this = right after this and because of it · turn into for a complete change (It turned into a big snake!) · tell + person + to + base verb for a reported instruction (Allah told Moses to go to Egypt and show … and warn …) · became for a new role · Then / Once more for the order of commands · the command → action → result pattern (imperative → past simple → result).
Notice (Activity 1): Read the last sentence “Upon this, Moses (pbuh) headed to Egypt.” Ask: “What came first? What did Moses do as a response?” Learners explain “Upon this” with their own words before choosing.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose turned into / to go / became, then order the mountain scene using Then and Once more and label each part command, action or result.
Likely errors: *told Moses go · *It turned to be a big snake · *Moses become a prophet · reading “Upon this” as a place.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about someone who receives instructions, carries them out, takes on a new responsibility and begins a new task.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Keep command, action and result in separate meaning groups: “PUT DOWN your WALKing STICK! | MOses put DOWN his STAFF on the GROUND. | It TURNED INto a BIG SNAKE!”
The reported mission is one long rising chain with a fall at the end: “alLAH TOLD MOses to GO to EGypt ↗ | and SHOW the PHARaoh the SIGNS ↗ | and WARN him … ↘”.
Stress the role change: “MOses beCAME a MESsenger of alLAH, | a PROphet.”
Word focus: THUN-der-ing (/θ/), SI-lence, MES-sen-ger, SHIN-ing, GUID-ance. Read Allah’s words calmly and respectfully.
beforeReading: Lesson 1: draw three columns (Command / Action / Result). Recall the fire from Chapter 8 and ask: “What do you think Moses will find there?” Keep the answers as predictions.
duringReading: Lesson 1: fill the two chains (staff, hand) in the three columns.
Mark the sentence where the mission starts (Show these signs to the Pharaoh).
Underline “told Moses to” and “became”.
Box the last sentence and ask what “Upon this” refers to.
afterReading: Lesson 1: complete the Quick Challenge and leave a bridge note: One command → action → result chain.
Lesson 2: Language Focus: Discover “Upon this” (Activity 1), choose turned into / to go / became (Activity 2), order the scene with Then / Once more (Activity 3).
Write five sentences about a new responsibility (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 Recall the fire from Chapter 8 and predict, three empty columns on the board; 5–15 Listen to the chapter (audio or the teacher, calmly), then read silently; 15–25 Pairs fill Command / Action / Result for the staff and the hand, each cell with a quoted phrase, whole-class check; 25–32 Mission boundary: Pairs find where the chapter moves from the signs to the task (Show these signs …, Allah told Moses to go …) and draw a line in their notebooks; 32–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note: One complete chain; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve both chains from the bridge notes; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (What came first? What was the response?); 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners report one school instruction with “The teacher told us to …”; 22–33 Use: A five-sentence paragraph about someone who gets a new responsibility (a team captain, a class representative) with an instruction, told … to …, became and a final next step; 33–38 Pairs check the “told + person + to” sentence and the verb after “became”; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What result follows each command?
Where does the chapter move from the signs to the mission?
What changes when the chapter says Moses “became a Messenger of Allah, a prophet”?

Stop the audio at “Allah said, ‘These are signs of My power.’” to mark the new phase.
Do not imitate the voice or act out the signs; keep attention on the wording and its function.

formativeAssessment: Builds both command → action → result chains accurately.
Separates the signs from the reported mission.
Explains “Upon this” and uses told + person + to and became correctly.
expectedResponses: Allah told Moses to put down his staff, and it turned into a big snake; then his hand came out shining like silver but not harmed. Allah told him to go to Egypt, show the Pharaoh the signs and warn him. After this message Moses became a Messenger of Allah, and upon this he headed to Egypt.

content.teacherReflection: Did the two-lesson split keep the sacred content calm and precise while still leading to real B1 production?

Where do you draw the line? (where the signs end and the task begins)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Make sure the sacred words are read calmly and not changed. Check that both chains are complete. In Lesson 2, listen for told + person + to in the reported school instruction.

objectives: Follow the order of Moses’s approach: explanation → every effort → realisation → continued refusal → signs → laughter.
Explain why the chapter says Moses “had no choice but to display the miracles”.
Discover “have no choice but to”, and rephrase After + -ing, kept + -ing and in order to (After he had made …, again and again, so that they could …).
Contrast the purpose of the signs (to help him against the Pharaoh) with the reaction of the king and his advisors.
content.pedagogy: Use a staircase of approaches on the board: TRIED (told him about Allah, explained, made every effort) → Realized (logical discussions would not work) → CHANGED (displayed the miracles) → RESULT (the king and his advisors laughed). Learners climb the staircase with evidence. The discovery question is: “Did Moses want to show the miracles first? What does ‘had no choice but to’ tell us?”
priorKnowledge: Past simple sequence, “realize that” and purpose with to + verb.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The signs do not come first: Explanation and every effort come before them. The laughter is the king’s reaction, not a sign that the miracles were weak; the chapter calls them “miracles of Allah”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: have no choice but to + base verb (only one option is left) · realized that + would not (a conclusion about the future seen from the past) · After + -ing = After + subject + had made · keep + -ing = again and again · When + past simple for the moment of a result (When he took his arm out, it was shining white!) · in order to = so that + subject + could.
Notice (Activity 1): board “Moses (pbuh) had no choice but to display the miracles.” Ask: “Did he have many options? Why was only one action left?” Learners find the reason in the two sentences before it.
Build (Activities 2–3): Order the actions and results using Then / When, then rewrite After making, kept refusing and in order to.
Likely errors: *had no choice but display / but displaying · *kept to refuse · *in order to helping · *After make every effort.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a person who tries one solution, realises it is not working, chooses another action, sees a result and explains the purpose.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Say the key phrase as one chunk with weak “to”: “had NO CHOICE but to (/tə/) disPLAY the MIRacles”.
The realisation with a pause: “MOses realized | that loGIcal disCUSsions | would NOT WORK.”
Stress the repeated refusal: “The PHARaoh KEPT reFUSing …”.
Word focus: com-PAN-ion, U-ni-verse, con-VINCE, LOG-i-cal, MIR-a-cles, ARM-pit.
beforeReading: Ask: “When you try to solve a problem and your first method fails, what do you do?” Collect two neutral examples (a password that does not work, a friend who does not answer messages).
duringReading: Mark every attempt Moses makes before the signs.
Underline the realisation and the refusal.
Box “had no choice but to”.
Mark the stated purpose of the signs and the reaction of the king separately.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge with the staircase.
Language Focus: Discover “had no choice but to” (Activity 1), order actions and results (Activity 2), rephrase effort, repetition and purpose (Activity 3).
Write five sentences about a change of approach (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: “Your first method fails. What next?” two neutral examples; 4–11 Listen and read, learners count Moses’s attempts before the signs; 11–18 Staircase on the board built by pairs: TRIED / Realized / CHANGED / RESULT, each step with a quoted phrase, and one pair explains the purpose of the signs; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Why was only one action left?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 30–37 Use: Learners write five sentences about solving a real problem (a broken projector, a team that cannot agree) with After …ing, realized that, kept …ing, had no choice but to and in order to, then pairs swap and find each structure; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Moses try before showing the signs?
Which sentence explains why only one option was left?
How does the chapter contrast the purpose of the signs with the reaction of the king and his advisors?
interactiveTips: Use the Harun hotspot for the visit to the palace and the Signs in the Palace hotspot for the two signs.
Replay the sentence with “had no choice but to” and the two sentences before it.
Report the laughter; do not act it out.

formativeAssessment: Keeps the correct order: Effort before signs.
Explains “had no choice but to” with evidence.
Rephrases After + -ing, keep + -ing and in order to correctly.
expectedResponses: Moses told the king about Allah and made every effort to convince him, but he realized that logical discussions would not work because the Pharaoh kept refusing. So he had no choice but to display the miracles: His staff turned into a big snake and his arm came out shining white. The king and his advisors laughed at him.

content.teacherReflection: Did learners explain the change of approach from evidence, and did they discover the meaning of “had no choice but to” from the sentences around it?

content.chapter: Chapter 11: The Miracle of the Staff
objectives: Keep the chapter’s distinction: The magicians’ sticks and ropes “looked just like snakes”, Moses’s staff “turned into a huge snake”.
Compare the magicians’ changed response with the king’s continued refusal, and give the reason the chapter states (because he was arrogant).
Use once, who-clauses, let + person + base verb, the imperative with “be”, still, because and continued to + verb.
Connect humility with changing one’s view after clear evidence.
content.pedagogy: Lesson 1 builds two columns, APPEARANCE (looked just like) and REAL CHANGE (turned into), and then two responses to the same event: The magicians who witnessed the miracle / the king who still refused. Lesson 2 opens the language: Learners discover that “look like” describes how something seems, correct three forms and then see how “still”, “because” and “continued to” show that the king did not change.
priorKnowledge: “Look like”, “turn into” from Chapters 9–10, “who” for people and “because”.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Looked just like snakes” does not mean they became snakes; the king himself calls it “only magic”. The Pharaoh’s refusal is explained in the chapter (he was arrogant) and continues after the magicians believe; keep his harsh orders factual and do not act them out.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: look (just) like = seems vs turn into = real change · Once = as soon as · who-clause for people (The magicians who witnessed this miracle …) · let + person + base verb (let those who worshipped Allah live) · imperative with be (Be rude to them!) · still for a refusal that continues · because + clause vs because of + noun · continued to + base verb.
Notice (Activity 1): board both sentences: “… they looked just like snakes!” / “… it turned into a huge snake.” Ask: “Which one is a real change? Which word tells you? What does the king call it?”
Build (Activities 2–3): correct which → who, to live → live and Being → Be, then complete still / because / to trouble and explain why “already” and “because of” do not fit.
Likely errors: *looked like = became · *The magicians which witnessed · *let them to live · *Being rude to them! · *because of he was arrogant.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a non-story turning point in which one group changes its view and another person keeps resisting.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress on the two verbs: “they LOOKED just LIKE SNAKES” / “it TURNED INto a HUGE SNAKE”.
Keep the who-clause together: “The MAgicians who WITnessed this MIRacle | BOWED DOWN …”.
Stress persistence: “The KING STILL reFUSED … | because he was ARrogant.” “He conTINued to TROUble …”.
-ed endings: witnessed /t/, refused /d/, worshipped /t/, continued /d/.
Word focus: MA-gic, ma-GI-cians, WIT-nessed, AR-ro-gant, WOR-shipped.

content.lessonPlan: Lesson 1 (40 min): 0–5 LOOKED LIKE / TURNED INTO with the toy car and ice examples; 5–15 Listen and read; 15–24 Pairs sort the chapter’s descriptions into the two columns, each with a quoted phrase, and find the king’s own words (This is only magic); 24–32 Two responses to one event: Groups of four make a T-chart (the magicians / the king) with evidence, then compare with the next group; 32–37 Quick Challenge; 37–40 Bridge note: One appearance sentence and one real-change sentence; Lesson 2 (40 min): 0–4 Retrieve the two columns and the T-chart; 4–12 Language Focus Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Which is a real change?); 12–22 Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners make one “let + person + verb” sentence about school rules (Our teacher lets us …); 22–33 Use: A five-sentence paragraph about a neutral turning point (a new rule in a club, a science experiment) in which one group changes its view and one person still refuses, with who, still, because and continued to; 33–38 Pairs check each other’s “still” and “because” sentences; 38–40 Exit ticket.

objectives: Separate Moses’s plan (We are going away, We will leave at night) from his rules (Get ready, you must keep it secret, Nobody should see us).
Explain why the caravan moves slowly without blaming the children and the old.
Discover the difference between plan forms and rule forms, and rephrase cause–result (That’s why → so) and success (managed to → succeeded in + -ing).
Analyse Moses’s reassurance (Calm down! … will show us the way to safety) as a response to a real danger.
content.pedagogy: Put Moses’s words to his people on strips and let pairs sort them into PLAN and RULES before they listen to the rest. Then build a chain on the board: Could not walk fast → moved slowly → the Pharaoh caught up → panic → reassurance. The discovery question is: “Which sentences tell people what is going to happen, and which tell them what they must do?”
priorKnowledge: Must / should, will, the present continuous for plans, could not for past inability.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The slow speed is not the fault of the children and the old; the chapter simply states that they could not walk fast. Moses’s reassurance does not deny the danger: The people can see the army.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: the plan with the present continuous and will (We are going away from Egypt. We will leave at night.) · rules with the imperative, must and should (Get ready …, you must keep it secret, Nobody should see us) · could not for past inability · That’s why = so for a result · manage to + base verb = succeed in + -ing · the imperative and will for reassurance (Calm down! … will show us the way to safety).
Notice (Activity 1): pairs sort Moses’s five sentences into PLAN and RULES. Ask: “Which forms tell the plan? Which ones tell people what to do or avoid?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Join the cause and result with so, rewrite “managed to catch up” as “succeeded in catching up”, then match the chase words with their meanings.
Likely errors: *must to keep · *Nobody shouldn’t see us (double negative, Turkish “kimse görmemeli”) · *managed catching · *succeeded to catch.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a non-story group that must leave quietly, has members who cannot move quickly, is followed and receives reassurance from its leader.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Plan and rules with different tones: Calm and informative for the plan (“We are GOing aWAY from EGypt.”), firm for the rules (“you MUST keep it SEcret.”). “must” is strong here: /mʌst/.
Limitation → result: “The CHILdren and the OLD | could NOT walk FAST … | THAT’S WHY | the CARavan moved SLOWly.”
Reassurance with a calm fall: “CALM DOWN! | alLAH is WITH us | and will SHOW us the WAY to SAFEty.”
-ed endings: panicked /t/, noticed /t/, managed /d/, prepared /d/, reached /t/.
Word focus: CAR-a-van, SE-cret, PAN-icked, SAFE-ty, AR-my.
beforeReading: Ask: “Your class is going on a trip and some classmates cannot walk fast. How should the plan change?” Collect two answers.
duringReading: Sort Moses’s words into PLAN and RULES.

Language Focus: Sort plan and rules (Activity 1), rephrase cause–result and success (Activity 2), match the chase words (Activity 3).
Write five sentences about a difficult group plan (Activity 4).
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook: The class-trip question, two answers on the board; 5–10 Strip sort in pairs: Moses’s five sentences into PLAN / RULES before listening; 10–17 Listen and read, pairs check their sort and continue the chain (could not walk fast → moved slowly → caught up → panicked → reassurance) with quoted phrases; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–29 Language Focus: Activity 1 now confirms the strip sort and learners name the forms themselves, Activities 2–3 in pairs; 29–37 Use: Groups of three plan a school evacuation drill or a quiet museum visit with a slow group, each learner writes five sentences (a plan with will, one must, one should, could not … that’s why, a calm reassurance), the group chooses the clearest paragraph to read aloud; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Which of Moses’s sentences give the plan, and which give rules?
Why did the caravan move slowly, and why is that not anyone’s fault?
What makes Moses’s answer to the panic calm and responsible?

Allah is with us and will show us the way to safety.”

objectives: Order the final events: trapped → command → the stick touches the sea → the path → the crossing → the Pharaoh’s claim → the sea closes.
Attribute “The sea opened at my order” to the Pharaoh as his claim, not the narrator’s account (Allah made a path for them across the sea).
Distinguish the story’s events from the general lessons in the last paragraph, and discover the two uses of “when” (one moment vs every time).
Use When, order + object + to + verb, lessons for us to learn, remind us that and to + verb for purpose in a final synthesis.
content.pedagogy: The final chapter needs two lessons. Lesson 1 secures event order and claim ownership: Learners label every sentence EVENT or CLAIM and see that the narrator says “Allah made a path”, while the Pharaoh says “at my order”. The drowning is stated once, factually. Lesson 2 moves from story to lesson: Learners discover that “when” with the past simple marks one moment, while “when” with the present simple and “always” states a general truth, and they build a final event → lesson paragraph.
priorKnowledge: When-clauses, past simple, “remind” and purpose with to + verb.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Pharaoh’s words about the sea are his claim; the narrator attributes the path to Allah. The last paragraph states general lessons (no one can enslave another human being, the only power over human beings is Allah); learners should not add lessons the text does not state. Keep the drowning non-graphic.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: When + past simple for one moment that triggers the next event vs when + present simple + always for a general truth (when we pray to Him, He always guides us) · order + object + to + base verb (Allah ordered the sea to close) · the final consequence (The sea closed over them, and they drowned.) · lessons for us to learn (noun + to + verb) · remind us that + clause for a general truth · sent prophets to + verb for purpose.
Notice (Activity 1): board the two when-sentences side by side. Ask: “Did this happen once in the story, or does it happen every time? Which verb forms tell you?” Learners formulate the difference before answering the true/false item.
Build (Activities 2–3): Order the crossing from command to consequence and label the trigger, the result and the reported order, then complete to learn / that / to.
Likely errors: *ordered the sea close · *lessons for us learning · *It reminds that no one … (remind needs a person: reminds us that) · *sent prophets for show.
Use (Activity 4): five connected sentences about a non-story situation where a leader gives an instruction, an event changes the situation, a consequence follows and the group explains what it learned.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Trigger and result in two meaning groups: “WHEN the STICK TOUCHED the WAters of the SEA, | a MIRacle HAPpened!”
The Pharaoh’s claim read neutrally, with the speaker clear: “the PHARaoh … SAID, | ‘LOOK! The SEA OPened at MY ORder.’”
Slow down at the move to the lesson: “It aGAIN reMINDS us | that NO ONE can enSLAVE | anOTHer HUman BEing.”
-ed endings: trapped /t/, touched /t/, parted /ɪd/, walked /t/, drowned /d/ (one syllable, not “drown-ded”).
Word focus: MIR-a-cle, MID-way, en-SLAVE, VIS-i-ble, PHYS-i-cal.

mediationTasks.lookFor: The retell is calm. Learners name the lessons in their own words.

thinkAloud.sentence: It also shows that the only power over human beings is Allah.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: I want to sum up the whole book in one sentence. The cruel king said he was a god, but the sea closed over him. My sentence is: Only Allah has real power, and He guides those who pray to Him. Learners sum up the next paragraph in one sentence.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Allah made a path for them across the sea!”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What did the Pharaoh say when he saw the road in the sea?
