metadata.title: Moses (B1) Teacher Guide
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned guide with chapter-specific support, inductive grammar and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 13 chapter units: Chapters 1–8, 10 and 12 are planned for 40 minutes; Chapters 9, 11 and 13 are planned as 40 + 40 minutes. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: B1 English learners, especially upper-secondary students.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow a connected narrative, locate evidence, track time, cause, contrast, purpose and viewpoint, and produce short connected explanations with support.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the story of Prophet Moses (pbuh) as told in this book, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter and without adding claims from outside the text.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does (the rule is confirmed only afterwards), then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. Chapters 9, 11 and 13 are divided into two 40-minute lessons rather than compressed. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 13 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks and production, exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Language Focus: Noticing and controlled practice

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs, with a short chapter-specific prediction, card set, route or question.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist, then read and follow the chapter’s own evidence structure: time frame, source and claim ownership, route, cooperation, two-day sequence, scene change, before/after help, background and event, command → action → result, change of approach, appearance vs real change, plan vs rules, or event vs lesson.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world. In 40 + 40 chapters, Lesson 1 secures meaning and evidence and Lesson 2 develops language and production.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise chapter Word Notes and the words the chapter’s key relationship depends on (accidentally, did not have to, had no choice but to, looked like, turned into).
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, image, hotspot or audio before any direct explanation; use a quick Turkish check only where a false friend or L1 pattern causes errors (3000 yıl önce → 3000 years ago, gerek yoktu vs izin yoktu).
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus production, exit tickets and the whole-book review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? Did it happen? Is it a real change?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practise it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: placing the story in time vs moving it on; feared that … would; make + person + verb / were made to; So / That’s why; continued to
Ch2: will for prediction (will be born); When / Then; imperative; so … that; was scared that … could; what to do
Ch3: passive focus (was carried away by); but / also / while + -ing / Soon; who-clause between commas; will for a decision
Ch4: care and belonging words; to + verb (purpose) vs because of / because (reason); will be; became; willing to
Ch5: while + past continuous vs past simple; saw; who-clause; understood that; what spoken lines do (imperative, present perfect, going to)
Ch6: be going to from present evidence; knew that; past simple chain; where / who; Wh-question word order
Ch7: did not have to (not necessary); cannot; So; until; That’s why ↔ because / as / since; there are no ↔ do not have any
Ch8: background (was, past continuous) vs main events; Suddenly; After + -ing ↔ After + had lived; because ↔ so; to ↔ so that … can
Ch9: Upon this; turn into; tell + person + to; became; Then / Once more; command → action → result
Ch10: have no choice but to; realized that … would not; After + -ing ↔ had made; keep + -ing; in order to ↔ so that … could
Ch11: look like vs turn into; Once; who-clause; let + person + verb; Be …!; still; because vs because of; continued to
Ch12: plan (present continuous, will) vs rules (imperative, must, should); could not; That’s why ↔ so; manage to ↔ succeed in + -ing
Ch13: when for one moment vs when … always for a general truth; order + object + to; lessons for us to learn; remind us that; to + verb for purpose

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, sequence, changes of speaker and meaning-bearing forms.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify direct evidence, track relationships across sentences and separate character claims from the narrator’s account.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain cause, contrast, obligation, change and consequence with chapter evidence, and transfer chapter language to the learners’ own world.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using chapter patterns, evidence and clear claim ownership.

valuesFocus: D1 Justice — reject oppression and judge power by how it treats people
D6 Honesty — represent evidence accurately and admit mistakes
D10 Humility — change one’s view when the evidence is clear
D11 Freedom — no one can enslave another human being
D12 Patience — live and work with patience through long or difficult periods
D14 Respect — disagree without ridicule and preserve human dignity
D16 Responsibility — take responsibility for mistakes, tasks and group decisions
D20 Helpfulness — recognize need from evidence and respond with concrete help
languageFocus: Every one of the 13 story chapters has an active Language Focus set built as notice → build → use.
Use Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence: Ask what the form does before naming it.
Let learners answer first; the explanation shown after each answer confirms the rule they have found.
At B1 the last step is always connected production about the learners’ own world, not a retelling of the chapter.

For 40 + 40 chapters (9, 11, 13), use the second lesson for Language Focus and connected production rather than re-reading the whole story. After Chapter 13, follow the book: Knowledge Check → Vocabulary Challenge → Master Glossary → Language Review → Final Challenge.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: One evidence sentence at a time, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by combining more chapter patterns or adding a second evidence relationship, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful discussion
notes: Handle the killing of babies (Chapter 2), the accidental death (Chapter 5), the king’s harsh orders (Chapter 11) and the drowning (Chapter 13) calmly and factually: read once, never role-played, illustrated or expanded.

Allah’s words, Qur’anic verses (for example Moses’s prayer, Surah al-Qasas: 15–16) and prayers are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped, “corrected” or rewritten, and no learner performs the voice of Allah or of a prophet.
Keep reported and claimed information attributed: Ibn Abbas’s report of the dream, the advisors’ prediction, the Pharaoh’s self-image and his claim about the sea.
Use neutral, safe school or everyday contexts for transfer tasks about warnings, mistakes, conflict or pursuit.
Do not add legends, dates, places or details about Moses, his family or the Pharaoh that are not in this B1 book, and do not present a learner’s reflection as a new religious claim.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Moses in this book links an ancient setting with questions every society still faces: How people are treated at work, how children and vulnerable people are protected, how strangers are welcomed and how a group moves forward when not everyone can move fast.

themes.title: Freedom and fair work:
themes.description: The Pharaoh made the Children of Israel do dangerous work for little or no money (Chapter 1), and the book ends by reminding us that no one can enslave another human being (Chapter 13). Discuss fair pay and safe work today.

themes.title: Protecting children together:
themes.description: A mother, a sister and a queen each act to protect one baby (Chapters 3–4). Discuss who protects children in a community today and how their roles differ.

themes.title: Welcoming a stranger:
themes.description: Moses arrives in Midian as a stranger who urgently needs a job and a house, and a family offers him work (Chapters 6–8). Connect this with how newcomers are welcomed at school or in a town.

themes.title: Noticing need and helping:
themes.description: Moses understands from the sisters’ own words that they need help and acts at once (Chapter 7). Discuss how to notice what others need without guessing from appearance.

actions: Write a short welcome guide in simple English for a new student at your school.
Plan a class trip that works for everyone, including classmates who cannot walk fast.
Find one example of a rule that protects workers or children in your country and explain it in two sentences.

exitTicket: One event from today’s chapter, with the sentence that proves it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week that shows a value from the chapter is …

miniProject.title: A Welcome Guide for a Newcomer
miniProject.desc: In groups, imagine a new student arrives at your school as a stranger, like Moses in Midian (Chapter 8). Make a one-page guide or a short audio clip in clear English: What the newcomer has to do on the first day, what they do not have to worry about, who can help them and why. Use at least three Language Focus patterns from the book, for example “have to / did not have to”, “because / so” and a “who” clause.

reflectivePrompt.title: Admitting a Mistake
reflectivePrompt.desc: In Chapter 5, Moses causes harm he did not intend. He says, “I didn’t do it on purpose. I have wronged myself,” and asks for forgiveness. Write six to eight sentences about a time when you or someone you know made an unintended mistake. What happened? How did the person respond? What did everyone learn?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values genuinely supported by the chapter. Require evidence first, then connect the value to an observable, age-appropriate action. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D1 Justice / D11 Freedom
items.value: Justice and freedom appear through the rejection of forced work and the final lesson that no one can enslave another human being.

items.label: D6 Honesty / D10 Humility
items.value: Admitting a mistake (Chapter 5) and changing one’s view after clear evidence (Chapter 11) are treated as concrete choices.

items.label: D9 Compassion / D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Care becomes visible through protecting a baby, noticing the sisters’ need and planning for slower members of a group.

items.label: D12 Patience / D16 Responsibility
items.value: Patience and responsibility appear in the simple life in Midian, in carrying out a mission and in calm leadership.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect means disagreeing without ridicule; the laughter and mockery in Chapters 10–11 are analysed, never imitated.

questions: Which part is source evidence and which part is your own application?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B1. The table links the B1 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B1 to the chapters of this book where learners practise them.

rows.descriptor: Can read straightforward factual texts on subjects related to his/her field and interest with a satisfactory level of comprehension.
practice: Chapter 4 (Back to His Mother): Fill the three columns with one action and one quoted phrase each.
Chapter 11 (The Miracle of the Staff): Lesson 1: sort each description under LOOKED LIKE or TURNED INTO.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write straightforward connected texts on a range of familiar subjects within his field of interest, by linking a series of shorter discrete elements into a linear sequence.
practice: Chapter 2 (The Pharaoh’s Dream): Write five connected sentences about a warning and a response in a safe setting (Activity 4).
Chapter 9 (The Voice on the Mountain): Write five sentences about a new responsibility (Activity 4).
Language Review, “Use: A Plan That Needed Help”: Write 5–6 sentences about a hard job you did with others. Tell a partner first.

rows.descriptor: Can reasonably fluently sustain a straightforward description of one of a variety of subjects within his/her field of interest, presenting it as a linear sequence of points.
practice: Chapter 2 (The Pharaoh’s Dream): Describe a safe warning situation: What someone predicted, what instruction followed, how people felt and one responsible next action.
Chapter 8 (A Simple Life in Midian): Explain a change of plan using a duration, a decision, a background sentence, a sudden event and a purpose.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (45 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (25 minutes): on paper. Write an article for your school website about a person you admire. (100–130 words)
Speaking (about 8 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Give the three women their own role: The queen asks for a nurse, the sister acts immediately, the mother becomes the nurse.
lookFor: Instruction: In groups of three, each learner is the expert on one woman. Find her action and a quoted phrase and report it to the group. Then add the growth line together.
Check questions: How many women? (three, one each) / What do you report? (her action and a quote)

While learners work: Check that the sister, the mother and Queen Asiye each have the right action. In Activity 2, listen for WHY or WHAT FOR. In the Use task, ask partners to underline the reason and the purpose.
Evidence of “Actor accuracy”: Gives each action to the right person.

peerObservation.chapter: Chapter 9: The Voice on the Mountain
peerObservation.focus: Trace each command to Moses’s action and its result (put down → turned into a big snake, put your hand … → shining like silver).
lookFor: Instruction: Lesson 1: Listen calmly. In pairs, fill Command, Action and Result for the staff and the hand. Then draw a line where the chapter moves from the signs to the task.
Check questions: What are the three columns? (command, action, result) / Where do you draw the line? (where the signs end and the task begins)
While learners work: Make sure the sacred words are read calmly and not changed. Check that both chains are complete. In Lesson 2, listen for told + person + to in the reported school instruction.
Evidence of “Command-action-result evidence”: Builds both command → action → result chains with evidence.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.
Write down the rubric criterion that most learners had not yet reached and the support you gave.
Every three or four chapters, look at the grammar sequence of this book and plan one short recycling activity for a form learners still avoid.
Before the End-of-Level Test, read your notes and choose two chapters to revise with the class.
standardisation: Before scoring, read the B1 descriptors for written and spoken production in the CEFR table of this book.

With a colleague, score the same three writing papers on your own with the B1 writing bands (Task, Organisation, Grammar, Vocabulary). Then compare and talk about any criterion where your scores differ by more than one band.
Score one speaking test together in the same way: both listen, both score, then compare.
Keep one agreed paper for each band as a sample for later scoring.

selfAssessment.prompt: Chapter 3: Could learners do this by the end of the lesson: “Trace the route instruction → action → river → palace → Asiye’s decision with evidence”? Which stage of the lesson flow helped most, and which did not?
Chapter 5 is planned for 40 minutes. Which stage took longer than planned, and what did you move to the next lesson?
Before the pair or group work in Chapter 6, did you ask “What do you hold up?” How many learners could answer before they started?
In Chapter 13, how many learners were secure on “Event sequence”? What did you do for those who were not yet secure?

When you asked “What does a newcomer need first in a new country (work, a home, the language)?” in Chapter 8, did learners describe other cultures with facts or with stereotypes? Which words did you give them?

Which of the likely errors listed for Chapter 10 did you hear (*had no choice but display / but displaying · *kept to refuse · *in order to helping · *After make every effort)? Did you correct them during the activity or after it, and why?
Which app tools did your learners use with this book (audio, Word Notes, the exercises and their result codes)? Which one gave you the most useful information about their learning?
Read your reflection log for this book. What is one change you will make the next time you teach this book, and who will you share it with?

actionResearch.question: Do learners use who-clauses to add information about a person (Chapters 3 and 5) in their own retelling?
steps: Baseline: in the Chapter 3 transfer task, count learners who write one correct who-clause.
Recycle: in Chapters 5 and 11, ask learners to add one who-clause about a character.
Check: after the B1 End-of-Level Test, note item 17 (defining relative clauses) for the class in Score a test.
Decide: compare defining and non-defining use in the writing papers and plan one practice for the weaker one.

collaboration: Share your counts for defining relative clauses with another English teacher who uses this book, and agree on one activity to try in both classes.
Plan the Chapter 6 and Chapter 8 lessons on newcomers in Midian with the class guidance teacher, and link them to welcoming new students.

objectives: I can explain why the Pharaoh was harsh to the Children of Israel.
I can say how the chapter places the story in time and then moves it on.
I can link a reason and a result with so and “That’s why”.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Sort time expressions such as “in the 13th century BC” and “Years passed” into two groups (placing the story in history or moving it on), rewrite the Pharaoh’s fear as his own thought with will and the forced work as a passive with were made to, then choose So, That’s why and to rule to link a reason to its result and show that a situation went on.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: AN-ces-tor, KING-dom, dic-ta-TO-ri-al, des-POT-ic. Say the date clearly: The thirteenth century BC. Make a short pause after “That’s why” and stress rude and harsh.
content.lessonPlan: Before you read, look at the two hotspots. Who ruled Egypt, and who lived there as a large group? Listen once for the main idea: Why was there a conflict in Egypt? Read the middle of the chapter again and mark the sentence with “feared that” and the sentence after it.
discussionPoints: The Pharaoh’s fear made him cruel to a whole people. How can fear lead a person with power to treat others unfairly, and what could stop it?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Pharaoh” and “Children of Israel”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Go back to the middle of the chapter. Read the sentence with “feared that” and then the sentence with “That’s why”. Notice that the dream comes much later, after “Years passed”. Then try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say five connected sentences about a different historical situation. Set the time, explain a fear with feared that … would, link a cause to a result, and describe an action that was forced or that continued.

whatToNotice: The chapter moves from belief (the Children of Israel believed in Allah alone) to fear (the Pharaoh’s worry about his kingdom) and then to cruelty.
Notice “That’s why he was rude and harsh to the Children of Israel.” The words “That’s why” point back to the Pharaoh’s fear in the sentence before.
readListen: Before you read, look at the two hotspots. Who ruled Egypt, and who lived there as a large group?
Listen once for the main idea: Why was there a conflict in Egypt?
Read the middle of the chapter again and mark the sentence with “feared that” and the sentence after it.
Open the picture hotspots “Pharaoh” and “Children of Israel” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Beginning: Find when and where Moses (pbuh) lived, and what the Pharaoh believed about himself.
Middle: Find what the Children of Israel believed and what the Pharaoh feared.
End: Find two ways the Pharaoh treated them badly, and what he saw in his dream.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: vision, ancestor, harsh, kingdom.
“just like their ancestor, Prophet Abraham (pbuh)”: What did the Children of Israel share with Abraham (pbuh)?
Use harsh and kingdom in one sentence about a ruler you have read about.
content.quickChallengeGuide: The question asks why the Pharaoh was rude and harsh. The answer is in the middle of the chapter, in the sentence just before “That’s why”. Check when the dream happened before you choose.
wrongAnswerSupport: Go back to the middle of the chapter.
Read the sentence with “feared that” and then the sentence with “That’s why”.
Notice that the dream comes much later, after “Years passed”. Then try again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the Pharaoh’s fear in my own words?
Can I show the link between his fear and his cruelty with so or that’s why?
Can I tell which time words date the story and which move it on?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say five connected sentences about a different historical situation. Set the time, explain a fear with feared that … would, link a cause to a result, and describe an action that was forced or that continued.

thinkAloud.sentence: That’s why he was rude and harsh to the Children of Israel.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “That’s why” points back to the sentence before. The Pharaoh feared that this large group would take control of his kingdom. That is the reason for his cruelty. Find one more reason in the chapter and say it with “because”.

objectives: I can follow the chain of events from the dream to the Pharaoh’s cruel order.
I can describe the fear of Moses’s mother and what she did about it.
I can use will for a prediction and so … that for a result.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Decide what the advisors are doing when they say “A boy will be born” (making a prediction), put four events in order with When and Then, then fix three mistakes about the mother’s fear: so frightened, could hear and what to do.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: ad-VI-sor, NEW-born, HEART-less, FRIGHT-ened. The gh in frightened is silent. Read the order “Kill all the newborn boys of the Children of Israel.” with a strong, falling voice.
content.lessonPlan: Look at The Dream hotspot. What did the Pharaoh see, and who did the fire not harm? Listen once and follow the events in order. Read the end of the chapter again and underline three phrases that show the mother’s fear.
discussionPoints: The Pharaoh acted on a dream and hurt many families. Why is fear never an excuse for cruelty? What did Moses’s mother do with her fear instead?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “The Dream” and “A Mother’s Prayer”.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the chapter from the start and stop after each event. Look for “When he woke up”, “Then, the Pharaoh told his soldiers” and “Moses (pbuh) was born in that year”. Put the events in order again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write or say five connected sentences about a different situation in which someone receives a warning. Report what someone predicted, give a command, describe a fear and its result, and end with a response or a request for help.

whatToNotice: Each event causes the next one: a dream, a prediction, an order, the soldiers’ search, a mother’s fear and a prayer.
Notice “His mother was so frightened that she was unable to sleep at night.” So + adjective + that joins a strong feeling to its result.
readListen: Look at The Dream hotspot. What did the Pharaoh see, and who did the fire not harm?
Listen once and follow the events in order.
Read the end of the chapter again and underline three phrases that show the mother’s fear.
Open the picture hotspots “The Dream” and “A Mother’s Prayer” and connect each one to a sentence in the chapter.
findAnswerInStory: Beginning: Find what Ibn Abbas reported about the fire, and who the Pharaoh asked about the dream.
Middle: Find the advisors’ prediction and the Pharaoh’s order to his soldiers.
End: Find why the mother could not sleep and what Allah told her.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: advisor, newborn, broke into, pity.
“the soldiers who were heartless showed no pity”: What does heartless add to the meaning of pity?
Write one sentence with advisor and one with pity.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will put five events in order, from the dream to the mother’s prayer. Use the time words When and Then, and check each step in the text.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the chapter from the start and stop after each event.
Look for “When he woke up”, “Then, the Pharaoh told his soldiers” and “Moses (pbuh) was born in that year”.
Put the events in order again.
selfCheck: Can I tell the chain of events in five steps?
Can I explain why the mother was so frightened?
Can I use so … that and what to do correctly?

thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: I do not know “heartless”. The sentence says the soldiers showed no pity while families cried. So heartless means having no kind feelings. Do the same with another new word in the paragraph.
